(CNN) -- The space shuttle Atlantis crew completed its first spacewalk to upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope, a daylong act of grueling labor that featured the replacement and installation of key instruments. Spacewalkers remove a camera from the Hubble on Thursday. Astronauts John Grunsfeld and Drew Feustel removed the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and swapped it out with an updated model, a device that "will allow the telescope to take large-scale, clear and detailed photos over a wide range of colors," NASA said. But they had a tough time removing a bolt in that task, an issue that caused some concern for colleagues on the ground. They eventually released it. "OK, here we go. I think I got it. It turned. It turned. And it's turning easily now," Feustel said. "Very nice." In all, the repair mission took seven hours and 20 minutes, a hard day's work that ended at 4:12 p.m. EDT. "It turned out very well," lead flight director Tony Ceccacci said during a NASA briefing. The team also replaced a Science Instrument Command and Data Handling Unit, a computer that "sends commands to Hubble's science instruments and formats science data for transmission to the ground," NASA said. The team "installed a soft capture mechanism, a device that will allow future vehicles to attach to the telescope," NASA said. And they installed "a combination of locks and latches that will allow for faster opening and closing of the telescope doors during the third spacewalk." "This is a huge accomplishment," Preston Burch, Hubble Space Telescope program manager, said during a briefing. "Our first EVA day in more than seven years." EVA is the acronym for "extravehicular activity," the phrase for spacewalking. It was the first of five spacewalks scheduled during the 11-day mission in which the crew will work in the shuttle's cargo bay to upgrade and repair Hubble. Astronauts Michael Good and Mike Massimino will perform the next spacewalk on Friday. They will be installing gyroscopes and batteries.  Learn more about the Hubble repairs » . The mission is one of the most ambitious space repair efforts ever attempted. Atlantis launched Monday afternoon for NASA's fifth and final repair visit to the telescope.  Watch Atlantis lift off on Hubble mission » . After a two-day chase, the shuttle captured the telescope Wednesday with its robotic arm some 350 miles above Earth and pulled it into Atlantis' cargo bay for service.  Watch Atlantis snag the Hubble » . It's been seven years since the last space shuttle crew worked on the telescope, which has been latched to a rotating, "lazy Susan"-type device for five days of repairs and remodeling. A camera mounted on the shuttle's robotic arm, 200 feet from the telescope, is taking pictures of it -- the first time the telescope has been seen since March 2002. An umbilical line was connected to provide electricity from Atlantis to the telescope, according to NASA. Mission commander Scott Altman also will position the shuttle to allow Hubble's solar arrays to gather energy from the sun and recharge the telescope's batteries. The timeline for the spacewalks is so tight, there's a chance the astronauts won't get everything done, especially if they hit any snags. And that's a real possibility because some of the repairs they are attempting have never been tried before. NASA canceled an Atlantis mission to extend Hubble's operational life in January 2004 because the trip was considered too risky in the wake of the 2003 space shuttle Columbia disaster, which killed seven astronauts. That accident was blamed on a hole punched in the front of the wing by debris during liftoff. But public pressure and steps taken to increase shuttle safety led the space agency to reconsider. Hubble's "greatest discoveries," NASA says, include determining the age of the universe -- 13.7 billion years, discovering that "virtually all major galaxies have black holes at their center," and "providing evidence that the speed at which the universe is expanding is accelerating -- caused by an unknown force that makes up for more than 75 percent of the universe." CNN's John Zarrella and Kim Segal contributed to this report .

The excursion was the first of five planned spacewalks during **STS-125**, NASA’s last mission to Hubble before the retirement of the space shuttle fleet.

### A Tight Timeline for Atlantis

Atlantis launched from Kennedy Space Center on **May 11, 2009**, after years of planning and delays. The shuttle reached Hubble two days later, and the telescope was grappled and secured in Atlantis’ payload bay on **May 13**.

- **May 13:** Shuttle crew captures Hubble with the robotic arm.

NASA officials said the mission’s goal was to leave Hubble with enough upgraded equipment to continue operating well into the next decade.

### Difficult Work on an Aging Telescope

The first spacewalk quickly showed why the mission was considered one of the most technically difficult shuttle flights ever attempted.

Hubble was not designed to be easy to repair indefinitely. Astronauts working in bulky pressurized gloves had to remove tiny fasteners, handle delicate scientific instruments and work around hardware exposed to nearly two decades of extreme temperature swings in orbit.

During the camera replacement, the astronauts encountered a stubborn bolt on the old camera assembly. The problem forced them to spend extra time freeing the instrument before they could slide it out of the telescope. Such delays were expected, NASA officials had said before the mission, because astronauts were dealing with aging equipment and one-of-a-kind hardware.

The new camera was among the mission’s most important upgrades. **Wide Field Camera 3** was built to dramatically improve Hubble’s ability to study galaxies, stars, planets and the early universe.

The astronauts also worked on replacing Hubble’s **Science Instrument Command and Data Handling unit**, a critical electronics package responsible for formatting and transmitting science data. A failure in that system in 2008 had delayed the mission while NASA prepared a replacement.

### NASA Emphasizes Hubble’s Scientific Value

NASA managers described the servicing mission as a major investment in one of the agency’s most productive scientific spacecraft.

Hubble, launched in 1990, initially became famous for a flaw in its primary mirror. That problem was corrected during the first servicing mission in 1993, turning the telescope into one of the most important observatories in history.

Since then, Hubble has helped astronomers:

- Refine estimates of the **age of the universe**.  
- Discover evidence that the universe’s expansion is accelerating, linked to **dark energy**.  
- Capture the **Hubble Deep Field** and later deep-field images showing thousands of distant galaxies.  
- Study the birth and death of stars in unprecedented detail.  
- Examine the atmospheres of planets beyond the solar system.  
- Provide evidence that supermassive **black holes** sit at the centers of many galaxies.

NASA officials said the final repair mission was intended to keep Hubble scientifically powerful until its eventual successor, the **James Webb Space Telescope**, could take over some of the work of observing the distant universe.

### A Riskier Shuttle Flight

The Hubble mission carried unusual risks because Atlantis was flying to an orbit that did not allow it to reach the International Space Station as a safe haven in an emergency. As a precaution, NASA prepared a second shuttle, **Endeavour**, for a possible rescue mission if Atlantis suffered serious damage.

The concern stemmed from the 2003 loss of **Columbia**, which was destroyed during re-entry after its heat shield was damaged during launch. Since then, NASA required detailed inspection procedures and rescue planning for shuttle missions.

For STS-125, Atlantis’ crew inspected the shuttle’s heat shield after launch and again during the mission. NASA also had Endeavour ready on the ground in case a rescue became necessary.

### Five Spacewalks to Renew Hubble

The first spacewalk set the stage for an ambitious servicing campaign. Over the following days, astronauts planned to install new gyroscopes, replace batteries, repair the **Advanced Camera for Surveys**, repair the **Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph**, and add equipment to help future spacecraft safely deorbit Hubble at the end of its life.

Many of the repairs required astronauts to perform tasks never originally intended for spacewalks. Some instruments had to be opened in orbit, with astronauts removing dozens of small screws while preventing any debris from floating away.

Despite the challenges, NASA said the mission offered a rare opportunity: a final chance to restore and upgrade a telescope that had transformed modern astronomy.

If successful, the work by Atlantis’ astronauts would give Hubble a new lease on life — and give scientists years more of images and data from one of humanity’s most famous windows on the universe.

**HOUSTON —** Astronauts working outside the shuttle *Atlantis* pressed through one of the most delicate and dangerous repair campaigns ever attempted in orbit, overcoming a stuck bolt during a spacewalk to continue upgrading and reviving the Hubble Space Telescope.

The mission, flown by NASA’s shuttle *Atlantis*, was designed to give Hubble a final major overhaul and extend the observatory’s life for years. But the work has tested the crew with tight timelines, aging hardware, and the unforgiving reality of servicing a telescope never meant to be fully taken apart by astronauts wearing bulky spacesuit gloves.

During one of the spacewalks, astronaut **Mike Massimino** encountered a stubborn bolt while trying to access Hubble’s **Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph**, or STIS, an important instrument that had been out of service since a power failure. The bolt refused to come free, threatening to block the repair.

After repeated attempts failed, Mission Control and the spacewalk team approved an unusual fix: Massimino physically removed a handrail that was preventing access, breaking it free so the crew could continue. The improvised solution allowed the astronauts to get inside the instrument and proceed with the repair.

“Sometimes you have to improvise,” NASA officials said in effect, as engineers on the ground watched the high-stakes work unfold from Houston.

The stuck-bolt episode became one of the dramatic moments of the mission, highlighting both the difficulty of repairing Hubble and the value of astronaut servicing. Many of the telescope’s components were not designed to be replaced on orbit, especially at the level of detail required during this mission.

## Completed Repairs and Upgrades

Despite the difficulties, the *Atlantis* crew has completed a series of major repairs and upgrades intended to transform Hubble’s scientific capabilities.

Among the work already accomplished:

- **Installed the Wide Field Camera 3**, a powerful new camera designed to observe the universe in ultraviolet, visible, and infrared light.
- **Installed the Cosmic Origins Spectrograph**, a new instrument built to study the large-scale structure of the universe and the chemical makeup of distant galaxies and intergalactic gas.
- **Replaced gyroscopes**, critical devices that allow Hubble to point precisely at stars, galaxies, and planets.
- **Replaced batteries**, giving the telescope fresh electrical storage for operations when it passes through Earth’s shadow.
- **Repaired the Advanced Camera for Surveys**, one of Hubble’s most productive instruments, restoring key observing capability.
- **Worked on the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph**, attempting to bring the failed instrument back to life.
- **Installed new protective insulation panels** to help shield Hubble’s aging exterior from the harsh environment of space.

NASA said the completed work should leave Hubble more capable than ever, with new instruments and restored systems expected to support observations deep into the coming decade.

## More Spacewalks Planned

The astronauts’ work is not finished. Additional extravehicular activities, or EVAs, are planned to complete remaining repairs and equipment installations.

Future spacewalk tasks include finishing instrument repair work, installing additional protective panels, and ensuring that Hubble is left in the best possible condition before *Atlantis* releases the telescope back into independent orbit.

Each EVA requires careful choreography between the spacewalkers, the shuttle crew operating the robotic arm, and engineers on the ground. Astronauts must handle small screws, power tools, sharp edges, and fragile telescope components while orbiting Earth at roughly 17,500 miles per hour.

NASA has described the mission as one of the most complex servicing flights ever attempted.

## Why the Mission Was So Risky

The Hubble servicing mission was considered unusually risky because *Atlantis* could not take refuge at the International Space Station if the shuttle were damaged.

Unlike most late-era shuttle missions, which flew to the space station, Hubble orbits at a different altitude and inclination. That meant *Atlantis* could not simply dock with the ISS in an emergency.

The danger was especially serious because Hubble’s orbit is in a region with a higher amount of orbital debris. A strike from even a tiny piece of debris could damage the shuttle’s heat shield or windows. If *Atlantis* suffered serious damage, the crew would have limited options.

To reduce that risk, NASA prepared a rare rescue plan: shuttle **Endeavour** was placed on standby for a possible emergency launch. If *Atlantis* had been deemed unable to return safely to Earth, *Endeavour* would have launched to rescue the crew in orbit.

That contingency plan underscored the stakes of the mission. NASA officials acknowledged that sending astronauts back to Hubble carried real danger, but said the scientific payoff was enormous.

## A Final House Call for a Historic Telescope

Hubble, launched in 1990, has become one of the most important scientific instruments ever built. Its images of galaxies, nebulae, star clusters, and distant cosmic objects have reshaped astronomy and become cultural landmarks.

This mission is expected to be the final shuttle visit to the telescope. With the shuttle program nearing retirement, NASA has no further Hubble servicing flights planned.

If the repairs hold, the upgraded telescope will be able to probe some of astronomy’s biggest questions: how galaxies form, how stars are born and die, how planets evolve, and how the universe has changed over billions of years.

For now, the astronauts aboard *Atlantis* continue their work high above Earth, turning stuck bolts, aging parts, and risky spacewalks into a renewed future for one of humanity’s most famous observatories.
